consensus_summary: Consensus primary meaning is the winepress as vivid symbol of divine wrath and eschatological judgment: God/Messiah treads the wicked like grapes so that blood flows as wine (Isa 63; Joel 3; Rev 14, 19; Lam 1:15). Abundance/blessing (overflowing presses) and vineyard-furniture uses are attested secondary or context-specific alternatives; Christological ‘mystic winepress’ passion readings are traditional but not controlling in modern exegesis.
book_summary: Winepress is the vineyard’s reckoning in which a people’s fruit is pressed and rendered to the Owner, yielding one of two vintages: presses bursting with new wine when the grapes are good, or the growers themselves trodden in ‘the great winepress of the wrath of God’ (blood for wine) when the vintage is wickedness.
consensus_core_identification: Divine wrath/eschatological judgment enacted by treading the wicked
book_core_identification: Vineyard reckoning that presses a people’s fruit for the Owner, with dual outcomes of blessing or wrath
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats wrath-treading as the dominant symbolic core and abundance as a separate, usually literal or secondary agricultural sense; the book unifies both as co-equal vintages of a single reckoning process centered on the vineyard Owner, thereby expanding the symbol’s governing frame and elevating the positive case from alternative to constitutive half.
material_contradiction: None; the book retains the wrath/blood-treading texts and sense without denying them.
rationale: Both readings share the same scriptural referents for judgment and for overflowing presses. The book does not replace the consensus referent of divine treading; it embeds that referent inside a broader vineyard-reckoning category that also canonically includes the blessing outcome. This preserves the central imagery while materially widening extension and re-ordering primacy, which is refinement by broadening rather than equivalence, contradiction, or novelty.
strongest_objection: Consensus regards the wrath image as so dominant in prophetic-apocalyptic usage that pairing it as merely one of two equal ‘vintages’ under a vineyard-reckoning heading dilutes the primary symbolic force the tradition has settled on.
